robust

/roh-BUHST/ - the stress falls on BUHST · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Robust means strong and able to hold up under strain.

Only a robust router survives a houseful of teenagers streaming, gaming, and video-calling at once.

Worked Example

Reviewers called the study's finding robust for a simple reason: it survived every attempt to shake it. Drop the outliers, and the effect stayed; swap the statistical model, and it stayed; re-run the survey in a second country, and it stayed. Fragile findings die in the first re-analysis; this one would not budge.

Robust is the reviewers' exact word because it means strong and able to hold up under strain — here the strain is deliberate stress-testing rather than weather or wear. Solid or convincing would merely praise the finding; robust makes the stronger claim that pushing on it from any side fails to move it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

durable: Durable means built to last a long time — it measures lifespan, resisting slow wear rather than sudden shocks. Robust measures strength under strain: a robust bridge shrugs off an overloaded truck, while a durable coating simply refuses to wear thin year after year.

tough: Tough is the everyday word for hard to damage, and it stretches to cover anything from boots to steak. Robust is more specific and more systemic: strong under strain, still working while the strain continues. A tough phone case survives being dropped; a robust network keeps running while parts of it fail.

resilient: Resilient describes what bends and bounces back — it takes the hit, gives, and then recovers its shape. Robust makes a different claim: it holds up under the strain without giving way in the first place. A resilient system recovers fast from trouble; a robust one keeps working through it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

flimsy: so lightly made that the first strain snaps it

frail: weak in body or build, easily broken

Where it sits · how much punishment it can take — sturdy → robust → indestructible

sturdy vs. robust: Sturdy is solid under ordinary handling — a good stool — but it stops short of robust, which keeps working when conditions turn hostile.

indestructible vs. robust: Indestructible goes further than robust — a robust design survives hard use and bad luck, while indestructible claims nothing can break it at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — rob-

Root — rob-: oak; the hardest timber (Latin robur)

Suffix — -ust

Suffix — -ust: made of, full of (trimmed from the Latin adjective ending -ustus)

Put it together

Put it together: Rob- (oak, the hardest timber the Romans built with — Latin robur) + -ust (made of, full of — trimmed from the Latin ending -ustus): Latin robustus meant 'oaken' — made of oak, strong as oak — and English kept the tree inside the word. Later in this course you will meet corroborate, from the same root: to strengthen a claim with more evidence, oak added to oak.

Use the root in a new word: corroborate

Use the root in a new word: corroborate: A second witness corroborated her account, and the timeline finally held firm — you will meet corroborate again later in this course.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / technical

Robust started on bodies and timber but now does its best work on systems: robust engines, robust studies, robust supply chains — things that keep working under strain. Its unit-mate withstand is the verb side of the same idea: a robust design withstands abuse. For simple physical solidity, sturdy is the plainer word.
